title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its features are congenital obstructive uropathy and an abnormal facial expression, with facial grimacing when the patient attempts to smile (Wang et al., 1997; Daly et al., 2010). Patients have enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis and voiding dysfunction caused by neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). Daly et al. (2010) noted that the urinary bladder fails to void completely even though there is no anatomical obstruction of bladder outflow and no overt neurological damage. Affected individuals often have reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure. Aydogdu et al. (2010) noted that the condition occurs in both sexes.

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, one of which was consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had peculiar facies and gestures while smiling and crying, together with hydronephrosis, hydroureter and intravesical stenosis of the ureter. Other findings included abnormal caliber of the urethra in its prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal bladder with trabeculation and diverticula. The bladder showed severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes.

paragraphs.text: Between 1965 and 1986, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) saw 36 children who had enuresis and urinary tract infection together with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. On urologic work-up, all patients had characteristic findings of mild neuropathic bladder, and most had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: Derbent et al. (2009) reported the first published case of urofacial syndrome in Turkey. The patient had been followed for recurrent urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux and was diagnosed with the syndrome at 16 years of age. The authors described the inverted facial expression, in which patients appear to cry when they smile. They noted that the urinary tract problems, including enuresis, urinary tract infection and hydronephrosis, are variable and can progress to hypertension and end-stage renal disease.

paragraphs.text: In contrast, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) concluded that urofacial syndrome is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Their evidence was multiple affected sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity and an equal sex ratio. Later reports also described the disorder as autosomal recessive (Wang et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2003). Pang et al. (2010) and Daly et al. (2010) found that it is caused by loss-of-function mutations in HPSE2, which were homozygous in the families studied by Daly et al. (2010).

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) carried out a genome screen in 20 selected UFS patients using homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling. Marker D10S677 was linked to and associated with UFS. Patients had a significant excess of homozygosity at this marker compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)), and allele frequencies differed between the patient pool and the control pools. All 31 patients studied were homozygous for 2 closely linked markers, D10S1726 and D10S198, which lie about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677. Only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinations at the flanking markers D10S1433 and D10S603 placed the gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.
